Oil Jumps 2% as Saudi Attacks and Tanker Strikes Revive Hormuz Fears
Oil prices climbed to their highest levels in nearly two weeks on Monday morning as fresh attacks on Saudi Arabia and oil tankers near the Strait of Hormuz put Middle East supply risks back at the center of the market, outweighing President Donald Trump's announcements of additional Russian diesel supplies and a Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire.
West Texas Intermediate was trading at $93.78 per barrel, up $1.93, or 2.10%, on Monday morning, while Brent crude rose $2.09, or 2.00%, to $106.80 per barrel, according to Oilprice.com data.
The renewed buying followed a weekend of attacks on Saudi Arabia, including a Houthi strike on Riyadh's international airport on Saturday that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300. Further attacks were reported Sunday, while two tankers were struck near Oman and in the Strait of Hormuz.
The tanker attacks threaten to interrupt the recovery in Gulf oil exports , which reached 81% of prewar levels in September. Crude and condensate shipments had recovered to 91%, but refined-product exports remained at just 60%.
Goldman Sachs raised its December Brent forecast to $90 per barrel from $85, estimating that geopolitical risks are currently adding just over $20 per barrel to oil prices.
The price increase comes as OPEC has sharply reduced its expectations for global oil demand growth this year. OPEC Secretary General Haitham Al Ghais said Monday that the producer group now expects demand to grow by just 400,000 barrels per day in 2026, down from the 1.4 million bpd it forecast at the beginning of the year.
OPEC expects much of the demand deferred during this year's disruptions to return in 2027. The group had already cut its 2026 growth estimate to 380,000 bpd in September, meaning Monday's 400,000-bpd figure is actually a slight increase from last month's forecast even though it represents a 1-million-bpd reduction from OPEC's outlook at the beginning of the year.
The International Energy Agency expects an even deeper demand hit this year, forecasting a 2.5-million-bpd decline in global consumption in 2026 followed by a 2.6-million-bpd rebound in 2027.
Additional Russian barrels could put some downward pressure on fuel prices. Trump said Friday that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons , or roughly 2.25 million barrels, of diesel to U.S. and global markets, with additional supplies to follow. Moscow has also partially lifted restrictions on diesel exports, allowing another 500,000 tons, or about 3.7 million barrels, onto the international market.
Trump also announced Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop attacking each other's energy infrastructure. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Russia of violating the agreement on Monday.
In the Gulf of Mexico, Shell , Chevron and BP were preparing to restore offshore production after Hurricane Isaias disrupted operations over the weekend.

items.title: Iran sets crosshairs on ‘US-UAE’ oil shuttle out of Strait of Hormuz - Al Jazeera

Share Iran sets crosshairs on ‘US-UAE’ oil shuttle out of Strait of Hormuz on social media
Ships float anchored off the coast of Khasab in Oman’s Musandam Governorate, near the Strait of Hormuz, on October 2, 2026 [AFP]
Tehran, Iran – Iranian authorities have signalled they intend to disrupt an Arab-operated and United States-assisted shuttle system that has enabled more energy exports through the Strait of Hormuz during the US-Israel war on Iran.
With the US naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports in place and sanctions tightening, Tehran has said it will pursue military and diplomatic efforts to put pressure on Washington to submit to its demands regarding reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

This strategic waterway, through which roughly a fifth of global oil and gas flowed before the war, has been largely closed to shipping following Iranian attacks since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28.
But the US Navy has reportedly opened up a route so Gulf states can export oil and other commodities amid an energy crisis.
Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei responded on Sunday night, saying the shuttle system is now an explicit target for Tehran.
Rezaei claimed that the US Central Command, with the assistance of the United Arab Emirates military, was using smaller vessels to transfer oil to larger tankers. He claimed Iran had been striking five or six participating vessels nightly for weeks.
“You are smuggling, but the strait is under Iran’s control, and we manage it,” he asserted.
This appeared to be a taunt aimed at US President Donald Trump, who has hailed energy exports at times reaching pre-war levels over recent weeks.
Rezaei appeared to give the impression that Iran wants to have lasting authority over Hormuz, and promised a harsh response if Iran’s energy and civilian infrastructure were attacked again.
His threats appeared aimed at Arab regional states, with a warning that digital infrastructure could be targeted. Rezaei threatened US-linked cables, data centres and artificial intelligence facilities in the UAE and around the Strait of Hormuz.
A woman rides her scooter past Iranian Zolfaghar missiles placed in front of a billboard of Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei at Baharestan Square in downtown Tehran, Iran, September 28, 2026 [Abedin Taherkenareh/EPA] Rezaei also accused Saudi Arabia of helping the US move oil around Iran’s restrictions. But he did not threaten a direct attack against Riyadh – which is currently being targeted by Yemen’s Tehran-aligned Houthis.
In early September, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) threatened tankers at ports and anchorages in Kuwait and Bahrain, citing US attacks on Iranian tankers . It accused both countries of complicity through hosting US armed forces.
Iran has claimed the US accepted some of Tehran’s seven conditions for the full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and ending the war. But Tehran insists that a deal will only materialise when all its demands are met.
Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst at the Crisis Group, said this reflects Tehran’s apparent assessment that it is under no immediate pressure to reach an agreement with the US since its pressure in the Hormuz has a global impact.
“The question, however, is whether Tehran is overestimating its ability to sustain this pressure, given the growing economic costs of the confrontation for Iran itself,” Azizi wrote on X.
The system involves very large crude carriers (VLCCs) and smaller vessels coordinating with the US military to load crude oil at Arab ports and use southern corridors near the coast of Oman to exit the strait.
Vessels often switch off their transponders and travel at night to minimise the risk of being targeted by the Iranians. After ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, some of the shuttles come back to load more.
Multiple vessels were targeted overnight Sunday to Monday, including two outbound tankers and one in anchorage near Oman’s port city of Sohar, where ship-to-ship transfers are allegedly being conducted.
Other vessels were targeted by projectiles last week, indicating that attacks have extended beyond the Strait of Hormuz to target the shuttle system.
The IRGC has also increasingly driven a narrative that naval mines, believed to have been planted across the Strait of Hormuz since the start of the war, pose a serious threat to vessels attempting to navigate the waterway without coordinating with Iran’s Persian Gulf Strait Authority.
The IRGC said three tankers suffered major damage over the weekend after being struck by mines. It also released footage of one ship ablaze that is said to have been struck by a mine, although the footage did not appear to show a mine going off.
The shuttle system has provided Arab national oil companies with a way out of Hormuz via the southern corridor near Oman.
Michelle Wiese Bockmann, a London-based senior maritime intelligence analyst at Windward, said this system has proven highly effective.
“Under international maritime law, which underpins 11 billion tonnes of seaborne trade annually, vessels have what’s called the right of transit passage,” Bockmann told Al Jazeera. “So, what Oman has done is allow vessels to go through under international maritime law, but they have had US military assistance.”
Tehran says shipping will be disrupted so long as the US continues its choking naval blockade against Iran, which has also stepped up its efforts to counter efforts by Arab states to export oil. At least 15 ships are believed to have been targeted in October so far, according to Winward.
“The more effective the route has become in facilitating the transport of oil and gas, the less leverage Iran has over Hormuz, and more attacks we are seeing on vessels that are using that southern corridor,” Bockmann said.
Windward’s data shows 31 ships transited the Strait of Hormuz daily in the final week of September. This was considerably lower than the 138 before the war.
Eighty-seven percent of the 45 ships targeted by Iran during the third quarter of 2026 were tankers.
Around 47 percent belonged to Gulf Arab energy companies’ national shipping fleets, Windward noted, and 93 percent of the strikes took place in the Strait of Hormuz. Most attacks targeted vessels transiting the southern corridor with their transponders turned off.
These attacks have contributed to a massive increase in freight costs. Freight represented 25-30 percent of Gulf crude’s cost, versus just 1 to 3 percent before the war, according to Windward. National oil companies have resorted to offering discounts of up to $35 per barrel below official selling prices.
The main reason for the rise is a shortage of tankers willing to make the dangerous crossing. Between 15 and 20 percent of very large crude carriers (VLCCs) are tied up with an inefficient logistics system that relies on shuttle transfers, complicated by escalating attacks and exposure at loading ports and anchorages.
“This is having cascading impacts for all vessel classes on freight and values across the world,” Bockmann said.

U.S. stock futures edged higher late Sunday after a drop in oil prices, following U.S. President Donald Trump's announcement that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an "energy ceasefire" effective immediately.
As of 11:27 p.m. EDT, Dow futures were up about 0.34%, the S&P 500 futures gained 0.31% and the Nasdaq-100 futures climbed 0.43%.

On Friday, the three benchmark indexes closed higher . The Dow Jones Industrial Average led the climb, adding more than 400 points to close up 0.83%. The S&P 500 gained 0.59% at close, while the Nasdaq Composite was up 0.64% at the end of the session.
Last week, all three U.S. benchmark indexes closed higher.
koyfin_20261012_083501091.png Key US Market Drivers
Oil was in focus late Sunday amid the dualities of an energy ceasefire announced between Russia and Ukraine and continued Middle East conflict, which kept prices above $100 a barrel.
Trump announced in a Truth Social post, "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!"
Earlier on Friday, Trump said that Russian leader Vladimir Putin had agreed to supply diesel to America and the global markets following a discussion. "Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter. Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel," Trump said.
Oil prices edged lower at the time of writing, although they continued to trade over $100 a barrel. Brent crude futures expiring in December were trading at $102.91 a barrel, down nearly 2%, while WTI crude futures expiring in November traded at $90.03 per barrel.
However, the deal with Russia was met with backlash from Republican and Democratic lawmakers, who said that it violates U.S. laws.
On Sunday, a group of seven senators, including four Republicans and three Democrats, released a statement urging the administration to "immediately reverse course."
"Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's brutal war against Ukraine. Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies. President Trump's decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law," they said.
"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," they added.
Meanwhile, conflict in the Middle East continued to escalate over the weekend after the Houthis claimed ‌responsibility ⁠for a Saturday strike on Riyadh's international airport that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.
Additionally, BP withdrew from the World Petroleum Council Energy Congress in Riyadh on Sunday after the attack.
"We made every effort to participate in WPC. ‌Unfortunately, ⁠due to travel disruption, we are unable to be there in person. We greatly value our longstanding partnerships across the region," a BP spokesperson ​reportedly said, as per Reuters.
The telecom sector was also in focus after SpaceX (SPCX) said it had agreed to buy up to 14 megahertz of paired spectrum in the 800 MHz band, putting Starlink Mobile on track to compete as a major U.S. mobile carrier.
Shares of other telecom companies including AT&T Inc. (T), T-Mobile US (TMUS), Verizon Inc. (VZ) and Comcast (CMCSA) sank following the announcement.
Meanwhile, investors are gearing up for the third-quarter earnings season, which starts next week with major U.S. banks reporting results.
IREN Ltd. (IREN): Shares of the company jumped 9% in the overnight session late Sunday after a media report indicated that Anthropic is the mystery AI cloud customer that IREN had referenced in its earnings call a few months ago.
WF Holding Limited (WFF): The microcap company drew retail attention after its shares pulled back overnight after jumping more than 499% on Friday amid speculative trading.
Verastem Inc. (VSTM): The biopharmaceutical company was in the spotlight ahead of its investor event on Wednesday, where it is expected to present initial efficacy results and updated safety data for its oral cancer drug.
Cipher Digital Inc. (CIFR): The company's shares moved 2% higher in the overnight session on Sunday, riding in sympathy with peer IREN's steep climb higher.
Among ETFs tracking benchmark indexes, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) and the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) all climbed at the time of writing, with sentiment in the 'bullish' territory.
Meanwhile, U.S. long-dated Treasury yields continued above 5%. At the time of writing, the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield was trading at 5.242%, and the 30-year Treasury bond yield was 5.60%.
The iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (TLT) was up 0.18% amid 'bullish' sentiment.
Asian markets opened mixed on Monday. South Korea's KOSPI, Japan's Nikkei 225 and China's SSE Composite were down at the time of writing, while Australian stocks were trading higher at the open.

As attacks continue to mount on shipping vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz, a seafarer's union official says some crews are being offered big rewards for making the crossing.
JOEL ROSE, HOST: President Trump blames the Russia-Ukraine war for soaring energy costs. The war with Iran, though, is the dominant factor keeping global diesel prices high. This weekend, the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations Centre reported several oil tankers traversing the Strait of Hormuz were attacked. Nearly a hundred vessels have been hit since the U.S. war with Iran began, resulting in two dozen deaths, according to the U.N. And the attacks are taking on new forms. MANOJ YADAV: Small boats that surrounded a few of the vessels and started firing with RPG and even with the guns. ROSE: Manoj Yadav is the general secretary of a union representing merchant sailors from India - many of whom work in the Persian Gulf. He says because of that danger, ship captains and sailors making these transits are being offered big money. YADAV: Not only one time, two time, three times - five times of their salary they are getting just to transit the Hormuz Strait. ROSE: Five times their regular salary. YADAV: Yeah. ROSE: And if they don't comply, Yadav says they might be punished. YADAV: And maybe there are possibility that they will get blacklisted. ROSE: Now, oil deliveries through the Strait of Hormuz have recently seen a recovery, maybe as much as 80% of the pre-war supply, according to trade intelligence firm Kpler. But the cost of getting through the choke point continues to hit pocketbooks around the world. And in the U.S., that's raising the political stakes ahead of the midterm elections.

OPEC Cuts 2026 Oil Demand Growth Forecast to 400,000 bbl/d | Egypt Oil & Gas
OPEC Cuts 2026 Oil Demand Growth Forecast to 400,000 bbl/d
OPEC expects global oil demand to grow by 400,000 barrels per day (bbl/d) in 2026, down from its initial projection of 1.4 million bbl/for, as market developments over the course of the year have prompted a reassessment, OPEC Secretary General Haitham Al Ghais said on October 12, Reuters reported .
The organization expects some of the demand postponed this year to shift into 2027, potentially supporting stronger consumption next year.
Addressing the 25th World Petroleum Congress (WPC) in Riyadh, Al Ghais also projected that global primary energy demand would rise by 23% by 2050, according to Investing.com .
He also warned that insufficient investment across the energy supply chain, from production to refining, was already having consequences, particularly for refining capacity, Investing.com reported.
The 2026 World Petroleum Congress (WPC) opened in Riyadh on October 11 as part of Riyadh Energy Week, which runs through October 15. The event brings together energy industry leaders, policymakers, and experts from around the world to discuss major challenges facing the sector, explore emerging technologies, and examine the future of global energy markets.

items.content:
Microsoft will mainly use its Maia chips for AI inference
Microsoft said it will eventually have multiple gigawatts worth of its Maia AI chips.
The company intends to make Maia its primary architecture for running AI models.
The next-generation Maia 300 chip enters production in 2027.
Microsoft will ramp up use of its homegrown artificial intelligence chips after years of reliance on Nvidia's graphics processing units, as the software giant attempts to bolster its AI stack.
Starting with its third-generation Maia AI accelerator, unveiled on Monday, Microsoft said it will mainly rely on its own silicon to handle incoming requests.
Microsoft's greatest strength in AI has been its Azure cloud, which runs a series of models for clients. Its Microsoft 365 Copilot and GitHub Copilot offer AI-powered services to software engineers and other office workers. And the company develops in-house models, though they've yet to make a big splash in a market dominated by OpenAI , Anthropic and Google .
The emerging opportunity in chips stems from unrelenting demand for advanced processors and a desire in the market for choice. Nvidia's GPUs have been the standard for AI workloads and models, and they fill Microsoft's existing data centers, while also serving to train models from OpenAI and Anthropic.
But as demand keeps growing, the model leaders have embraced a variety of silicon from companies including Amazon , Advanced Micro Devices , Cerebras , Google and, in recent months, Microsoft.
For general-purpose use, Microsoft already taps its own central processing units as well as silicon from Intel and AMD . Finance chief Amy Hood said at a Goldman Sachs conference last month that use of its own chips has helped with "margin improvement over the course of a decade."
Microsoft introduced its inaugural AI chip, the Maia 100, in 2023 . It touted the Maia 200 this past January , and CEO Satya Nadella told analysts in July that Maia 200 "delivers 30% better performance per dollar than the latest generation hardware in our fleet" and said it was handling OpenAI models.
Production of the Maia 300 starts in 2027. Microsoft is targeting multi-gigawatt deployments of chips in the Maia family, according to a blog post from Executive Vice President Scott Guthrie. But Alistair Speirs, a general manager, declined to provide a timeline.
"We reserve a little bit of optionality there, because this is an industry that's changing very fast, and we want to deploy the right silicon for the right models that we're using at the right time as well," Speirs said.
AI's quiet safety gatekeepers are stepping into the spotlight
Microsoft's Nadella says AI needs an 'emergency brake' that humans control
Nvidia GPUs are everywhere. Here are the ways companies are accessing them
Hollywood takes on Zuckerberg, Musk and Altman amid widespread anxiety over AI
Microsoft expects to pack 96 Maia 300 chips into each data center rack, double the number for the Maia 200. The new version can run through up to seven times more AI tokens per rack, with 40% more tokens per megawatt when compared with GPUs.
"We need new architectures that will give us essentially better performance, better use of the power that we have," Speirs said. "You can think of power translating pretty directly into operational cost for something like a data center as well."
Parts of Microsoft 365 Copilot should speed up with Maia 300, said Jim Kleewein, a technical fellow at the company.
In a note distributed to clients on Wednesday, Evercore ISI analysts estimated that Maia will represent about 10% of Microsoft's spending on AI chips by the first quarter of 2027. The analysts recommend buying Microsoft shares.
Nvidia will still be a big part of the equation. CEO Jensen Huang spoke at an event last week where Microsoft announced a Surface laptop containing an Nvidia processor. And when it comes to training models, Microsoft partners with Nvidia and AMD, Speirs said.
Unlike Google's tensor processing units or Amazon's Inferentia and Trainium, Microsoft's accelerators can't be rented by the hour to other companies.
"Nobody has tested them outside of Microsoft yet," said Patrick Moorhead, CEO of advisory firm Moor Insights and Strategy.

items.title: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and the FOMC Just Fired a Warning Shot at the Second-Priciest Stock Market in History - The Motley Fool
items.summary: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and the FOMC Just Fired a Warning Shot at the Second-Priciest Stock Market in History  The Motl
items.content:
This has been a year highlighted by a changing of the guard. Longtime CEOs Warren Buffett and Tim Cook handed over the keys to their respective successors, and President Donald Trump's Fed chair nominee, Kevin Warsh, became only the 17th head of the central bank on May 22.
Despite these changes, Wall Street's preeminent stock indexes, the Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI +0.39% ) , S&P 500 ( ^GSPC -0.09% ) , and Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC -0.40% ) have been unstoppable. The artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out and otherworldly growth prospects accompanying this game-changing innovation have lifted the broader market to new heights.
This won't be a one-and-done rate-hiking cycle. Image source: Official Federal Reserve Photo.
But sustaining this AI-driven bull market could be easier said than done. Last week, Fed Chair Warsh and his Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) colleagues fired an unmistakable warning shot at the second-priciest stock market in history. The only question is: How many investors are paying attention?
The Federal Reserve's rate-hiking cycle is ramping up
On Sept. 16, Warsh and 11 other voting members of the FOMC unanimously raised the federal funds target rate by 25 basis points to 3.75%-4.00%. It's just the fourth time this century that the central bank has kicked off a rate-hiking cycle .
Warsh and the FOMC have been compelled to act because of persistently elevated inflation. August marked the 66th consecutive month in which the annualized inflation rate topped the FOMC's long-term 2% target.
"The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long," https://t.co/htRQqyQHtr
While rising prices are perfectly normal in an expanding economy, inflation has soared in 2026 due to Trumpflation (inflation that's specifically driven by President Trump's policies). Donald Trump's tariffs are increasing domestic manufacturing costs, while the Iran war has led to the ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The largest energy supply disruption in modern history has sent fuel prices soaring.
The newly released Federal Reserve meeting minutes (effectively a summary of what policymakers discussed behind closed doors on Sept. 15-16) point to tariffs, the Iran war, and the AI infrastructure build-out as key sources of inflation.
More importantly, the Fed meeting minutes charted a path forward for interest rates. Contained in the Fed minutes was this statement:
With regard to the outlook for monetary policy beyond this current meeting, most participants assessed that another increase in the target range for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate by year end. While this statement doesn't tell us whether the FOMC would raise interest rates at the October or December meeting, it makes it crystal clear that additional rate hikes are expected in the not-too-distant future. That's terrible news for a historically expensive stock market.

A truly jaw-dropping amount of capital is being spent on the AI data center build-out , part of which has been financed with debt. If lending costs rise, as the FOMC's September meeting minutes imply, it could slow this expansion and adversely impact lofty growth expectations.
In June, the S&P 500's Shiller Price-to-Earnings Ratio came within a stone's throw of surpassing the priciest valuation multiple in 156 years , achieved just before the dot-com bubble burst. This is a stock market with little to no margin for error. If the Fed's rate-hiking cycle ramps up, maintaining this aggressive AI build-out without any "hiccups" would likely prove impossible.

Microsoft Stock Rises as Tech Giant Takes Aim at Nvidia's AI Chip Dominance
Microsoft MSFT shares rose 1% in Monday morning trading as the company outlined plans to shift more AI workloads to its own Maia chips, according to a company blog post published Monday.
Microsoft introduced Maia 300, the third generation of its custom AI accelerator, with production deployments due to start in 2027. It aims to expand the Maia family to multi-gigawatt capacity and fit 96 chips in each rack, twice the Maia 200 configuration. Maia 200 is already running production workloads, including Copilot, with GitHub Copilot and Microsoft Foundry expected to follow by year-end.
The company says Maia 300 could process up to seven times as many AI tokens per rack as its predecessor and deliver 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU systems. These efficiency gains could help address the computing and electricity demands of expanding AI services.
Nvidia chips will remain part of Microsoft's infrastructure, especially for training models, and Microsoft also uses processors from Advanced Micro Devices. Still, broader Maia deployment could give the software maker more control over costs and supply. Whether outside cloud customers will adopt Maia remains uncertain.

Stock Market Today: S&P 500 Futures Pause Near Record Highs as Oil Rises Ahead of Bank Earnings
Oil surging past $100 is lifting energy stocks while high bond yields drag on tech, and underneath a deceptively calm index, a quiet rotation is reshaping portfolios before bank earnings reveal whether the slowdown is finally catching up to borrowers.
A businessman observes the city skyline, symbolizing the broader economic landscape as markets anticipate the opening bell. The view reflects on a record-setting week while looking ahead to new market developments. © 24/7 Wall St.
S&P 500 futures are basically flat before the open. The index's futures sit near 7,817, up 0.1%, after a record-setting week. Oil is the main mover this morning. Brent crude is trading near $106 a barrel because the war with Iran is still disrupting global energy supplies, and that is raising oil stocks before the bell. Investors are holding the S&P 500 steady ahead of Tuesday, when bank earnings season begins.
Brent settled Friday at $105, and it keeps rising. In May, the EIA expected Brent to average $89 in the fourth quarter. Prices are still well above that forecast, so producers are making more per barrel than planners expected.
Exxon Mobil ( NYSE:XOM | XOM Price Prediction ) is up 1.2% in premarket trading. Chevron ( NYSE:CVX ) is up about the same, and both stocks have gained close to 45% this year. In midstream, Energy Transfer ( NYSE:ET ) agreed last week to buy Vaquero Midstream. The deal adds to a pipeline network that already carries natural gas to power plants serving AI data centers .
On Friday the 10-year Treasury yield rose to 5.2%. It recently reached its highest level since 2002. The Fed also raised its target rate in September, which sets the upper bound at 4%. Higher rates make future profits worth less today, and fast-growing tech stocks feel that the most.
NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA ) is down 0.4% before the open. That small dip matters because NVIDIA makes up 8% of the SPDR S&P 500 ETF ( NYSEARCA:SPY ), which is barely moving near $779.
The flat index hides money moving underneath it. Energy is gaining while the largest tech holding falls, so the two cancel out in the headline number. Owning an S&P 500 index fund means most of your results still depend on a handful of AI giants, and increasingly on the power, cooling, and pipeline companies feeding them (we highlighted seven of those suppliers in a free AI infrastructure report ). Oil exposure is cushioning those holdings right now, but it can't fully replace them.
The VIX, Wall Street's fear gauge, is around 15, which counts as a normal reading. Options traders are calm even though bond yields are at multi-decade highs and oil is above $100.
Four of the largest U.S. banks report before the open on October 13, along with two major health care companies. Watch the money banks set aside for bad loans. The economy added only 29,000 jobs in September, so rising reserves would show the hiring slowdown is starting to hit borrowers.

Balkan temperatures swing as heavy rain heads for Greece
Clear skies bring warm days and cold nights to Montenegro, while a low-pressure system moves towards Aegean Sea
Temperatures fluctuated dramatically in the Balkans last week, with unusually large differences between daytime highs and overnight lows – known as the diurnal range.
An area of high pressure over the region brought prolonged sunshine during the day, while clear skies at night allowed temperatures to drop rapidly as heat escaped into the atmosphere without cloud cover to slow the cooling.
In Kosanica, Montenegro , the average maximum temperature in October is 15C (59F), while the average minimum is 4C. However, on 4 and 5 October the difference between daytime highs and overnight lows reached 30C, more than double the October average.
Elsewhere in Europe , high pressure will build across the north and west over the coming week, pushing an area of low pressure southwards towards the Mediterranean. The low-pressure system will deepen as it crosses the Adriatic and Ionian seas before moving eastwards into the Aegean Sea by the middle of the week.
Spells of heavy rain and strong winds are expected to sweep across Greece as a result. Forecast models suggest widespread rainfall of 50-150mm, with the highest totals expected around the island of Skiathos.
Towards the end of the week, the system will continue eastwards, bringing showers to parts of Crete, which was hit by severe flooding a week earlier. Those storms swept some cars and trees into the sea.
People cross a bridge over a swollen river as Hurricane Simon approaches Mexico’s Pacific coast in Costalegre, Jalisco state. Photograph: Daniel Becerril/Reuters Meanwhile, Hurricane Simon, a category 4 storm, is moving close to Mexico’s Pacific coast, near the state of Jalisco. It is the latest of 21 named storms in the Pacific this season, 11 of which have reached hurricane strength.
At the time of writing, Simon has a central pressure of 933mb and maximum sustained winds of nearly 150mph (241km/h). However, the hurricane is expected to weaken rapidly if its core moves onshore, cutting it off from the warm ocean waters that fuel it.
Heavy rainfall is affecting south-western Mexico, where totals could reach 300-400mm across a wide area, rising to 400-500mm in the wettest locations.

Microsoft reveals Maia 300 AI chip as it works to reduce dependence on Nvidia, AMD
Microsoft ( MSFT ) has debuted its latest AI chip, the Azure Maia 300, as it looks to reduce its reliance on third-party processors from the likes of Nvidia ( NVDA ) and AMD ( AMD ).
Unveiled at the OCP Global Summit 2026 in San Jose on Monday, the Maia 300 will join Microsoft's Maia 200 and Maia 100 chips as part of what the company said will be multigigawatt deployments beginning next year.
The Windows maker said that will make its Maia chips the "primary AI inference system for Microsoft products and services."
The company said Maia 300 provides 40% more tokens per megawatt than "leading GPU-based systems," a clear swipe at Nvidia, and that a 96-chip rack offers seven times the rack-scale token throughput of Microsoft's Maia 200.
Tokens are a basic unit of measurement in AI systems that can represent parts of words, images, and videos.
The more tokens per megawatt, the more efficient an AI rack.
Microsoft's Maia 300 processor. (Image: Microsoft) · Microsoft The Maia 200 chip currently powers its Microsoft production workloads, including Microsoft 365 Copilot, as well as OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ) models, Microsoft's MAI models, and open-source models. That provides 1.7 times more tokens per watt for AI capabilities in Microsoft's Teams, Copilot, and Cowork software versus other GPU-based systems, the company said.
Microsoft and fellow hyperscaler peers Amazon ( AMZN ), Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ), and Meta ( META ), as well as AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ), either already offer or are working on their own custom chips.
Doing so acts as a hedge against becoming overdependent on processors from Nvidia and AMD. Producing their own semiconductors also allows companies to tailor them to their specific needs.
That's a potential problem for Nvidia, which regularly generates upwards of 50% of its quarterly revenue from hyperscalers.
On top of that, Amazon and Google now rent out their custom chips to third-party customers, a direct threat to Nvidia's business. What's more, Amazon is looking into selling chips for customers to install in their own data centers rather than running them from Amazon's own facilities.
That doesn't necessarily mean hyperscalers will stop purchasing Nvidia chips entirely. Customers still want access to a number of chips for different workloads, meaning the Amazons and Microsofts of the world will need to continue stocking up on the most in-demand processors.

items.title: Microsoft makes ‘biggest bet yet’ on its own silicon, unveils new AI chip to reduce reliance on Nvidia - GeekWire
items.summary: Microsoft makes ‘biggest bet yet’ on its own silicon, unveils new AI chip to reduce reliance on Nvidia  GeekWire
items.content:
by Todd Bishop on Oct 12, 2026 at 6:22 am October 12, 2026 at 6:24 am
A prototype of Microsoft’s Azure Maia 300 chip, which the company plans to begin deploying at scale in 2027. (Microsoft Photo)
Microsoft plans to run most of its AI services on chips it designs itself, a shift that could save the company billions of dollars and reduce its dependence on industry juggernaut Nvidia.
The company on Monday unveiled Maia 300, the third generation of its custom AI chip, saying it will begin large-scale deployments in 2027. In a blog post , Azure chief Scott Guthrie said Maia will become “the primary AI inference system for Microsoft products and services.”
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella called it “our biggest bet yet on our own silicon” in a post on X .
Maia 300 will produce 40% more AI output for the same amount of power as leading GPU-based systems, which Nvidia dominates, according to the company.
A full rack of the new chips will produce up to seven times as much AI output as the current generation, the company says. They’re designed for the kinds of tasks that are growing fastest, such as AI agents that work through multistep jobs and models that handle long documents or conversations.
The Redmond company designs the chips and relies on Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC) to make them, rather than buying finished chips from Nvidia. More-efficient chips also let Microsoft run AI services using less electricity, at a time when power supply has become one of the biggest constraints on AI expansion.
Microsoft and Nvidia remain big partners. Nadella and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang shared the stage last week to launch Windows PCs built on Nvidia chips. Nvidia also remains a key supplier for Microsoft’s data centers, and Nadella said on the company’s July earnings call that Microsoft will be among the first cloud providers to deploy next-generation systems based on Nvidia’s Vera Rubin and AMD’s Helios.
Microsoft’s move is part of a larger trend among tech giants to design their own AI chips. Google has started selling its Tensor Processing Units directly to some customers, and Amazon has won over AI companies including Anthropic with its Trainium chips. Meta has rolled out its own AI chips , and OpenAI unveiled its first custom chip , built with Broadcom, in June.
Microsoft has been playing catch-up. Unlike Google’s and Amazon’s chips, Maia isn’t available for outside customers to rent. Microsoft’s first Maia chip, announced in 2023 , was followed by a second-generation Maia 200 this January after delays. As of this summer, Maia 200 was running in just two U.S. data centers, The Information reported in August .
Maia 200, the current generation, already powers Microsoft 365 Copilot and runs models from OpenAI as well as Microsoft’s own. It’s now being deployed across the U.S., Europe and Australia, according to Microsoft. GitHub Copilot and Microsoft Foundry are set to move onto it by the end of the year.
The shift will take time. Evercore ISI analysts estimate that Maia will account for about 10% of Microsoft’s spending on AI chips by early 2027, CNBC reported .
Microsoft says it will share more details next month at its Ignite conference in San Francisco.

The new Maia 300 chip will start rolling out to production AI workloads in 2027.
The new Maia 300 chip will start rolling out to production AI workloads in 2027.
Tom Warren is a senior correspondent and author of Notepad , who has been covering all things Microsoft, PC, and tech for over 20 years.
Microsoft is announcing its third-generation Maia in-house AI chip today, designed to be the “primary AI inference system” for Microsoft’s products and services. Maia 300 not only improves the cost and efficiency of running AI workloads in the cloud, it’s also more capable of handling the latest reasoning models and agentic tasks.
Maia 300 will start being rolled out to production in 2027, and it has been designed with efficiency in mind. “We expect Maia 300 to deliver 40 percent more tokens per megawatt compared to leading GPU-based systems,” says Scott Guthrie , executive vice president of Microsoft’s cloud group. “And in a full 96-accelerator configuration, it delivers up to 7x the rack-scale token throughput of Maia 200.”
These efficiency improvements will allow Microsoft to rely mainly on its in-house AI chips soon, instead of ones from Nvidia and AMD. “We will scale our Azure Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027, making Maia the primary AI inference system for Microsoft products and services,” says Guthrie.
Maia 300 chips will start being used for production workloads in 2027. Image: Microsoft
Maia 300 is a successor to the 200, which was only announced in January . Maia 200 is already running on production AI workloads across Microsoft, including Microsoft Copilot, GitHub Copilot, Microsoft Foundry, and Microsoft’s own AI models.
“Maia 200 is the best performing AI infrastructure in our fleet, measured in real world metrics for AI services,” says Guthrie. “Maia 300 is a complete AI system designed for the new types of AI workloads emerging today: Long-context reasoning, latency-sensitive conversational experiences, and sustained, multi-step agentic tasks.”
Microsoft is finally making custom chips — and they’re all about AI
Microsoft’s latest AI chip goes head-to-head with Amazon and Google
Microsoft is using a new chiplet architecture to get its all-important efficiency gains. Built on TSMC’s N2P process node, the latest Maia 300 architecture separates compute, memory controller, and I/O functions. “This increases the silicon area dedicated to compute performance and allows each function to use the technology best suited to its role,” says the Azure hardware and infrastructure team.
Maia 300 is also a key part of Microsoft’s own AI model work, and could help the company achieve its goal of catching up with Google DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic. “We have to work across the full stack, all the way down to the silicon,” says Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman. “At that scale we need a platform that we own, and that we co-design with our models. That’s why running our Microsoft AI models on top of the Maia chip is a critical focus for our team.”

Microsoft challenges Nvidia with new Maia 300 AI chip promising 40% greater efficiency
Microsoft says its new in-house AI accelerator can generate 40% more tokens using the same power as competing GPU-based systems; deployment is set to begin in 2027, with the chip expected to become a central platform for the company's AI services
Microsoft on Monday unveiled Maia 300, a powerful new artificial intelligence chip developed in-house, along with a complete computing system designed to support it, as the technology giant steps up efforts to reduce its dependence on Nvidia and secure greater control over the infrastructure powering its AI services.
The company says the new chip and the system built around it can deliver 40% more AI output at the same level of electricity consumption as competing systems based on graphics processing units, or GPUs. Microsoft plans to begin deploying Maia 300 in 2027, when it is expected to become a central platform for running AI models across its products.
The announcement marks another step in the intensifying competition among technology giants to develop their own AI processors rather than rely heavily on Nvidia, whose chips continue to dominate the market for training advanced AI models.
Maia 300 is a specialized data center processor known as an AI accelerator. It was designed by Microsoft to run AI workloads in the massive data centers supporting its Azure cloud platform, with an emphasis on processing information quickly while using as little electricity as possible.
Microsoft is following a path already taken by Google, which developed its own Tensor Processing Units, or TPUs, and Amazon, which created its Trainium chips. All three companies are seeking to gain greater control over the hardware powering their growing AI operations.
For Microsoft, developing its own processors is also a way to prepare for surging global demand for AI computing power, reduce supply chain bottlenecks and secure a reliable supply of chips without depending entirely on external suppliers.
One of the main reasons behind Maia 300 is the rapid rise of AI agents, systems capable of carrying out complex tasks involving multiple steps rather than simply answering individual questions.
These agents require computing infrastructure capable of handling enormous amounts of information, responding quickly and operating efficiently over extended periods. Microsoft says Maia 300 was designed specifically for these increasingly demanding workloads.
From right: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella. The companies remain close partners even as Microsoft works to reduce its dependence on Nvidia's chips
Unlike chips primarily used to train AI models, Maia 300 focuses on a process known as inference. This is the stage at which an already trained model processes a user's request and generates a response.
Training involves teaching a model to recognize patterns and develop capabilities using vast amounts of data. Inference is what happens afterward, when that model is put to work answering questions, analyzing information or completing tasks.
Nvidia's processors still dominate the training market, but Microsoft is positioning Maia 300 as a more efficient alternative for inference, particularly as AI agents become more capable and their computing requirements grow.
According to Microsoft, the new accelerator and its supporting system can produce 40% more tokens at the same power consumption as competing GPU-based platforms. Tokens are the basic units of text that AI models process and generate, making token throughput a key measure of performance for AI services.
Another major focus of Maia 300 is reducing the time needed to move data between the different components of an AI computing system.
In large AI models, information must constantly travel between memory and processors, as well as between multiple accelerators working together. These transfers can create bottlenecks that limit performance even when the processors themselves are extremely powerful.
Microsoft says Maia 300 addresses this problem with an architecture designed to speed up data movement and improve efficiency across the entire system.
The chip provides memory bandwidth of 18 terabytes per second, allowing it to feed large volumes of information to AI models at high speed and support workloads that require substantial memory capacity.
The company says these capabilities will be particularly important for the next generation of AI agents, which will increasingly need to analyze extensive information, maintain context across long interactions and complete complex, multistep assignments.
Maia 300 is not Microsoft's first attempt to develop its own AI hardware. The company already operates an earlier system, Maia 200, which supports its Copilot AI assistant and the team developing its next generation of AI models.
Microsoft plans to expand the earlier system's use to additional services by the end of 2026, before beginning deployment of Maia 300 in 2027.
The transition reflects a broader shift in the AI industry. As artificial intelligence becomes embedded in everyday software and AI agents take on more demanding tasks, the cost of running models is becoming increasingly important alongside the computing power required to train them.
For Microsoft, the potential benefits extend beyond performance. Developing its own chips could reduce reliance on Nvidia, ease pressure on hardware supply chains and give the company more control over the costs and availability of computing resources.
The two companies remain major partners, with Nvidia's technology playing an important role in Microsoft's AI infrastructure. But Maia 300 highlights Microsoft's determination to build an increasingly independent hardware ecosystem.
Whether the new chip can meaningfully alter the balance of power in the AI semiconductor market will depend on how it performs once deployment begins in 2027.

Cleveland Fed's Beth Hammack backs smaller, more frequent rate hikes
The Cleveland Fed president said she prefers incremental policy adjustments over waiting and risking a larger correction later
By Cris Tolomia · 2 min read · Updated October 12, 2026
Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Beth Hammack said Monday that she favors making smaller, more frequent adjustments to interest rates rather than delaying action and potentially requiring a larger move later.
“When feasible, I generally think it’s preferable to make smaller adjustments, and to do so relatively quickly, rather than to wait and risk needing a larger course correction,” Hammack said in a speech at the National Association for Business Economics annual meeting in Cleveland.
Hammack, who votes on policy decisions this year, said she views inflation pressures as relatively broad-based rather than concentrated in any single component of the economy. A restrictive monetary policy stance is appropriate to ensure inflation returns to the Fed's 2% target in a timely fashion, she said.
Much of the speech centered on the value of transparency, with Hammack arguing that officials should articulate the logic behind their decisions — a so-called "reaction function" — while stopping short of offering "firm predictions" about where rates are headed. "I want to draw a sharp line here. A reaction function is not forward guidance," Hammack said, according to Bloomberg . "Treating the two as interchangeable can turn a well-meaning explanation of logic into the expectations of a promise."
Hammack also said that with each passing month, persistently elevated inflation raises the risk of an inflationary mindset becoming entrenched in the economy. She stopped short of backing a rate increase at the Fed’s Oct. 27-28 meeting, according to Bloomberg.
Hammack's preference for steady, incremental tightening reflects a position she has held for months. She argued in August that more than one rate increase would likely be needed to bring inflation back under control and that interest rates at the time were not placing meaningful restraint on the economy. She dissented at the Fed's July meeting, when the committee voted 9-3 to hold rates steady, preferring a quarter-point increase alongside Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari and Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan.
The Fed ultimately raised its benchmark rate by a quarter percentage point in September , a unanimous 12-0 decision that brought the federal funds rate to a target range of 3.75%–4%. The decision reflected a shared view among Fed officials that rising prices — fueled by the Iran war and surging demand connected to artificial intelligence buildout — required a policy response, according to Bloomberg. Sixteen of 18 meeting participants at that time projected at least one additional rate increase.

Stellantis and Renault back UK to get EU car industry protection
Bosses of Citroën owner and French carmaker also urge UK government to consider limiting imports from China
Stellantis and Renault have backed the UK car industry for inclusion in proposed rules to protect EU industry, but urged the British government to consider limiting imports of Chinese cars.
Emanuele Cappellano, who leads Stellantis’s European brands including Fiat, Citroën, Opel and Vauxhall, and François Provost, the chief executive of France’s Renault, said the UK should effectively be counted as one of the EU’s 27 member states for the purposes of the proposed “Made in Europe” legislation .
The new rules aim to ensure EU subsidies and government procurement benefits Europe’s industry, rather than helping manufacturers from other countries.
EU to limit Chinese hybrid vehicle imports to 350,000 a year
The executives were speaking at the Paris motor show, which was attended on Monday by the French president, Emmanuel Macron. Brands including Li Auto, GAC and Chery were among a host of Chinese manufacturers exhibiting in Paris with ambitious European expansion plans.
Europe’s car industry is under enormous pressure as it copes with lower demand than before the coronavirus pandemic, while also investing tens of billions of euros in shifting production to electric vehicles (EVs). At the same time, Chinese carmakers’ market share has soared as the transition to EVs opens the door to new entrants.
The EU confirmed on Monday it would limit the number of hybrid electric vehicles imported from China to 350,000 cars a year. The EU expects that the quota, which will come into force in December, will halve China’s market share, which now stands at 6% in a landmark four-year agreement made in Beijing last week.
The Made in Europe rules are another plank of the EU’s response to the rise of China in key manufacturing industries such as carmaking and chemicals.
Under the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), cars will have to be “made in Europe”, and contain enough European parts and materials, to continue to qualify for EV grants and to be bought by public bodies in the EU. However, automotive manufacturers and politicians are haggling over the details.
If Brussels sticks to a strict definition of “European” as being only EU countries, Britain risks being left out – prompting intense lobbying from UK car industry and government to be included.
Stellantis is among the manufacturers that still has a British factory, its facility in Ellesmere Port, Merseyside, which produces small vans.
“I think that UK somehow needs to be equalised to the EU 27,” said Cappellano, referring to the bloc’s 27 member states. “We have a lot of relationship, we have footprint. Historically UK has been very close to the European market.”
Europe’s main automotive lobby groups ACEA and Clepa have also put their weight behind the UK to be included. Some parts of European manufacturing, including France’s industry minister , had argued that the UK should be left out given Brexit.
Provost said there was “no other choice” but a deal between the UK and EU. However, he said the UK would also have to stop allowing Chinese cars in without limits.
“On your side, you have also to take decisions,” he said. “If the UK is willing to join the European ecosystem, this is to have an industrial ambition … to keep a strong automotive industry.”
He said this would be an industry that “is not closed to Chinese competitors, but … if you want to operate in Europe, you have to deeply invest in the whole value chain, final manufacturing, suppliers, R&D, technologies.”
Provost added: “I’m not here to demand whatsoever, but I think if UK is willing to join this ecosystem of IAA, there is some open question about the level of imports.”
London has so far rejected pressure to impose its own tariffs on Chinese imports, but the UK business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, this month said that decision was under review .
Cappellano also said the UK should consider imposing tariffs on Chinese imports. “It’s very important that the UK defines what is the priority,” he said. “It’s very difficult to defend industrial footprint and at the same time let the market completely open to import. Either one or the other.”
He expressed scepticism over whether other countries beyond the EU such as Japan, Turkey and Morocco should be included in the rules.
“We don’t necessarily need to have a larger definition of European scope,” he said, pointing to proposals that carmakers be allowed to source 30% of their materials from outside the EU.
He also argued for more time until 2030 for manufacturers to source batteries from within Europe. China is dominant in the global supply of batteries and Cappellano said it would take longer to build up the European industry.

items.title: Immigration agents search Congresswoman Ilhan Omar's home
items.summary: Omar, an outspoken Trump critic, said the search was "an attempt to target political enemies" and that she "will not be silenced".
items.content:
Figure caption, Watch: Agents seen outside US Congresswoman llhan Omar's home
US immigration agents searched the home of Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar on Monday morning as part of a "criminal investigation".
Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents "executed a judicially authorized search warrant" for the home in the Washington, DC, area, a US justice department spokesperson told the BBC.
The search "is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation," the spokesperson said, but no further details were given. US Congress is currently out of session and it is unclear if Omar was at the home.
Omar, an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump, described the search as "an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement."
"For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns," Omar said in an online statement. "This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced."
Her communications director Jacklyn Rogers called the raid "an outrageous abuse of power" by the Trump administration. "The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong."
The nature of the criminal investigation remains unclear. A BBC crew saw several agents at the home, some carrying boxes to a van. News of the search was first reported by Fox News, which has said the investigation is about immigration paperwork filed by her late father when Omar was a child.
The timing of Monday's raid â 22 days to the November midterm elections which will decide the balance of power in Congress for the next two years â has raised concerns from Democrats who have rallied behind Omar.
The justice department has a longstanding policy of refraining from most enforcement action that is "likely to raise an issue or the perception" it was being brought for the purpose of affecting any election or disadvantage a candidate.
The US House Democratic Party leadership said in a statment that Omar was targeted with "vile personal attacks and baseless accusations."
"Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family."
Omar's immigration records have been scrutinised in the past by Republicans. Earlier this year, fellow Congresswoman Nancy Mace of South Carolina unsuccessfully filed a subpoena of her records.
Last month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told a conservative podcaster "something is going to happen", making allegations of marital fraud against Omar. Separately, the White House border tsar Tom Homan told Fox News Omar was being investigated for unspecified immigration violations.
Omar, a Democrat, denied these allegations last month. "I will say it again so it's as clear as possible: I'm not at all worried about these investigations, because they are complete shams," she said in a campaign fundraising email, an archive of which has been seen by the BBC.
She has been targeted by Trump with the president previously suggesting that she "should go back" to Somalia and that she should be deported. US citizenship is required to serve as a US House Representative.
Omar has responded to Trump's insults and attacks describing them as an "unhealthy and creepy obsession."
The president also spoke unfavourably about the Somali American community. Last week, he wrote on social media that Minnesota "is being taken over by Somali immigrants" and said "the people of Minnesota must fight back."
Republicans celebrated the search. "Nobody is above the law," said Minnesota Representative Tom Emmer. "We look forward to learning more details about this raid and investigation. ACCOUNTABILITY IS COMING!"
Omar is the first Somali-American elected to the US House of Representatives and she represents a district in the Minneapolis area. She and Michigan Representative Rashida Tlaib were the first Muslim women elected to Congress.
Minnesota Governor Tim Walz also criticised the search on Monday. "Americans see this for what it is - President Trump is abusing his power to go after political opponents weeks before an election."
Minnesota senator Tina Smith said called it "a transparent attempt to interfere in our elections."

items.title: Pentagon Finally Counts an Iran War Death — Six Months Late - The Intercept
items.summary: Pentagon Finally Counts an Iran War Death — Six Months Late  The Intercept
items.content:
An Army carry team moves the flag-draped transfer case containing the remains of U.S. Army soldier Maj. Sorffly Davius, who died in Kuwait, during a casualty return on March 9, 2026, at Dover Air Force Base, Del.
The Pentagon quietly acknowledged additional Iran war deaths on Friday evening after The Intercept repeatedly demanded an explanation for inaccurate statistics on a War Department website tracking U.S. casualties from the conflict.
Almost 900 U.S. troops have been wounded or killed in the war with Iran, according to the official Pentagon count, including the two deaths added on Friday. This raises the Pentagon’s total to 21 dead.
The additional war dead include Maj. Sorffly Davius, a signals and communication officer with the New York Army National Guard who was assigned to the headquarters of the 42nd Infantry Division and died while on duty in Camp Buehring, Kuwait, on March 6. For more than six months, The Intercept has raised Davius’s case in dozens of emails and phone conversations with Pentagon officials and publicly in 10 articles.
The Pentagon recently revamped the website of the Defense Casualty Analysis System, or DCAS — which provides official counts of dead and wounded for Congress and the White House — to include more detailed casualty category tables. But it initially listed no “non-hostile” illness or injury fatalities, despite the Pentagon announcing in March that Davius died “as a result of a non-combat related incident.”
At first, the military claimed that Davius was involved in another operation instead of Epic Fury — the original designation of the Iran war. Two weeks ago, however, The Intercept revealed that a recent National Guard news release admitted that when “President Donald Trump made the decision to attack Iran and launched Operation Epic Fury on Feb. 28, the [42nd Infantry] division headquarters began conducting combat operations.” The 42nd served as the primary headquarters leading what became, according to Maj. Gen. Jack James, the division commander, the “largest and first long-range precision fires campaign in the history of the United States Army.” James specifically saluted Davius, whom the Guard admitted was “conducting operations” when he died.
Last week, The Intercept pointed the Pentagon to the non-hostile illness or injury casualty count for Epic Fury on the website, and emphasized its tally showing zero deaths was not possible.
“I will check within,” Patricia Kreuzberger, a Pentagon spokesperson said on Tuesday. “Let me reach out to leadership.”
Three days later, and after repeated follow-up messages on Friday, the tally was updated, to 1.

In addition to Davius, the DCAS death count now also includes an unidentified Navy suicide that occurred last month, according to a U.S. official who spoke on the condition of anonymity. DCAS currently lists this death as “pending,” despite the recent addition of a “self-inflicted” category to the website.
A “War Department official” told The Intercept by email on Sunday that “the Department is introducing a ‘Pending Adjudication’ category to track the status of active duty casualties pending final categorization and reporting in DCAS.” She added: “This new category will allow the Department to minimize reporting delays while ensuring data consistency between the DoW and Joint Staff.”
The “pending” designation, however, isn’t new. The Pentagon re-introduced it to DCAS in mid-July, and major discrepancies have continued in the tally since.
Many casualties remain uncounted in DCAS, including a sailor who suffered a  non-combat-related injury  aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln as it was involved in “strike missions in support of Operation Epic Fury” on March 25.
The Pentagon Found a New Way to Undercount U.S. Casualties in Iran
Most Iran war casualties in the official count — 454 personnel as of Friday — have occurred since July 7, after the Trump administration claimed the conflict ended. At that time, the Pentagon switched from counting casualties under Epic Fury to the anodyne moniker “Overseas Operations.”
The most recent casualties are three Army personnel wounded in action this month. The latest known Iran war fatality is Capt. Bianca Wilkerson, 37, of Norfolk, Virginia, who died on September 18 from a “coronary issue,” according to her brother. He said she returned from Saudi Arabia on September 10 and was headed back but died on the return flight, according to reporting by the Virginian-Pilot. A U.S. official told The Intercept that Wilkerson died “as a result of a non-combat-related incident,” but after nearly a month, DCAS still lists no non-hostile illness or injury deaths.
“There is no excuse for a mistake of this magnitude,” Reps. Chrissy Houlahan, D-Pa., and Adam Smith, D-Wash., said in a joint statement on Friday after the House Armed Services Committee discovered “a discrepancy in the Pentagon’s reporting of casualty numbers” and brought it to “the Trump Administration’s attention.” They continued: “The failure of Secretary Hegseth to immediately take ownership of the problem also does a grave disservice to the men and women putting their lives on the line in service to our country.”

For six months , The Intercept has reported on anomalies in official counts offered on DCAS. When the first ceasefire was struck between the Trump administration and Iran on April 7, the tally of U.S. casualties was 385. Despite a pause in hostilities, the number slowly rose to 428, according to Pentagon statistics. But on April 21, the number of  wounded-in-action troops declined by 15  without public acknowledgment by the War Department. Despite repeated questions for months, the Pentagon has not explained the adjustment.
Other discrepancies have also gone unjustified for months. An Army “illness/injury” death appeared on or about May 26 but disappeared by June 1. On July 20, the Pentagon repeatedly altered DCAS, adding 100 casualties to the war’s tally without explanation; the total number of wounded cited by DCAS on that date included counts of 413, 427, and 447. Three days later, the Pentagon dropped the Iran war death toll from 18 to 14. On July 22, DCAS added 10 recent casualties to the Epic Fury count. By July 25, those wounded personnel were dropped from the tally. They may have been added to the Overseas Operations casualty toll, but the Pentagon has failed to offer any explanations.

Prior reporting by The Intercept also found that the Pentagon’s official tally of dead and wounded personnel is a gross undercount, stemming from what one U.S. government official called, in April, a “ casualty cover-up .” When the Washington Post also suggested last month that the Pentagon had suppressed the casualty numbers, self-styled War Secretary Pete Hegseth called the report “DISGUSTING and FAKE.”
When asked by The Intercept about the Pentagon’s continued peddling of bogus statistics, Kreuzberger did not offer an explanation. An email from a nameless “War Department official” said: "We have nothing to provide beyond the Defense Casualty Analysis System website."

AMERICAN BUSINESSES AREN’T ALLOWED TO BUILD. IT’S TIME CONGRESS HELPED THEM
The fight to build this much-needed pipeline is now 10 years old. In April 2016, the state denied the water permit. Courts upheld it. The company tried again in 2025, then withdrew in November after three notices that its application was incomplete.
And the problem runs deeper than one pipeline. Ill-conceived climate laws set sweeping emissions targets, and the plan to reach them is thin if not unattainable. Take New York City's Local Law 97. It fines large buildings that exceed emissions limits, and the limits tighten sharply in 2030. Owners must pay for costly retrofits or pay penalties. Either way, the bill lands on tenants, co-op owners and small businesses.
THE REAL REASON YOUR ELECTRIC BILL IS SOARING THIS SUMMER WILL SURPRISE YOU
Democrats in too many state capitals seem determined to choke off other reliable and cost-effective energy sources. Nuclear reactors and coal plants have closed down, both of which supply much-needed energy to citizens, especially low-income families.
Meanwhile, the utility bills keep climbing , filling your gas tank becomes more painful, and truckers and shippers face punishing prices for diesel, which, of course, trickles down to raise the cost of everything from lumber to lunch meat.
SENATORS PRESS PRESIDENT TRUMP TO RELEASE HOME HEATING OIL RESERVES AMID SOARING PRICES
I’ve spent over 20 years in the energy and utility industry. Energy is not abstract. It is pipe, wire, steel and supply. Limit supply while demand holds, and prices rise. That is arithmetic, not ideology.
And winter makes it more brutal. On the coldest days, when pipes run full, utilities scramble for alternatives and alternatives cost more. Families on fixed incomes can't opt out. They lower the thermostat and pull on another sweater.
TRUMP ADMIN MOVES TO GUT BIDEN'S SIGNATURE ENVIRONMENTAL RULES
Here is what should bother everyone, whatever their politics. A state that won't produce or import its own fuel doesn't become independent. It becomes a customer. It bids against the world for supply and accepts whatever price is asked, including prices set by wars it can't influence.
The fight to build this much-needed pipeline is now 10 years old. In April 2016, the state denied the water permit. Courts upheld it. The company tried again in 2025, then withdrew in November after three notices that its application was incomplete.
What's the solution? Approve pipeline projects with capacity that bring in domestic gas. Keep reliable power plants running until real replacements are built and tested. Approve the construction of new refineries. Be honest about what climate mandates cost and phase them in at a pace working families can afford. Judge success by lower bills and steady supply, not ribbon-cuttings.
And most importantly: Vote for candidates this November who are dedicated to American energy independence , supporting sensible and robust expansion of both production and refinement of our own bountiful energy supply.
Dave Bovee spent 20 years in the energy and utility industry. His book, "The Four G Revolution: The Fight to Save God, Gas, Guns, and Glory," was published by RealClear Publishing on October 6.
